metadata.title: Textures and Color
metadata.audience: people making games in Godot, and anyone directing an AI that writes shaders for them
metadata.lecture_opening_description: How a shader reads images, and why colors shift
metadata.bookend_exempt_reason: lecture skill: opens on the narrated identity card then the hesitant writer; no composer cold open.
metadata.source_doc: Godot 4.7 documentation; Godot 4.7.2 runs on Apple M4 Pro (evidence/planning-checks); see SOURCES.md

beats.narration_text: Textures and Color. Learn how a shader reads a texture, how to do math on color, and why the color you type is not always the color you see.

beats.narration_text: Hallo. This is Liam, in for Bear. Most people picture a texture as a picture pasted onto a shape. A shader never pastes anything. For every pixel, it looks a color up in a table, by address.

show.event: backspaces 'pasted onto a shape' and types 'looked up by address'

props.text:
A texture is a picture
pasted onto a shape.

beats.motion_claim: The writer types the assumption a newcomer arrives with and corrects it into the film's real subject.

qc.sparse_reason: Hesitant-writer bookend: the correction is the motion.

beats.narration_text: Six terms. A shader is a small program the graphics card runs to decide how something is drawn. U V is a point's address on a shape, from zero to one across and down. A texture is an image a shader can read by address. A channel is one of red, green, blue or alpha. Alpha is how visible a pixel is: zero invisible, one solid. And the renderer is the part of Godot that draws.

terms.meaning: a small program the graphics card runs to decide how something is drawn
a point's address on the shape: 0 to 1 across, 0 to 1 down
an image a shader can read by address
one of red, green, blue or alpha
how visible a pixel is: 0 invisible, 1 solid
the part of Godot that draws

beats.narration_text: First, the table. A texture is a grid of colors, and every entry has an address: U V, zero to one across, zero to one down. Hand the table an address, and it hands back the color stored there.

shot.visual_intent: A 6-by-6 grid of cells: the cream letter F on teal (the film's tiny table), with a one-cell teal margin. Beside it a swatch box with four numbers under it, and under the grid an address readout '(u, v)'. A terracotta dot (the address) starts at the top-left cell, a thin line runs from the dot to the swatch, the swatch takes that cell's color and the four numbers fill in (0.98, 0.98, 0.96, 1.0). Labels: 'texture', 'address', 'color'.

show.event: dot on a cream cell: swatch cream, four numbers
dot on a teal cell: swatch teal (0.37, 0.64, 0.57, 1.0); settles through 60 %
dot on the next cream cell

shot.motion_claim: The address dot hops from cell to cell and, each time, the swatch changes to that entry's color.

qc.sparse_reason: Lecture body beat: one object or scene on a cream stage, the voice carries the explanation; only underfill/clustered are waived.

lecture.why: A grid with a moving address and a swatch that answers is the whole idea of a lookup, as motion; a render would show the result but not the asking.

beats.narration_text: In code, the lookup is one function: texture, then the table's name, then the address. It returns a color. Fragment runs once for each pixel, so every pixel asks with its own address, and the shape fills in.

shot.visual_intent: Code card at left (the four-line lookup shader); at right a real Godot window: a plain Color Rect that now shows the 8-by-8 teal and cream checker picture. A terracotta ring moves to one cream cell and then one teal cell, each with its address as a readout.

show.event: fragment line highlighted with its meaning
COLOR defined on the lookup line
ring on a cream cell, address (0.06, 0.06)
ring on a teal cell, address (0.19, 0.06)

cues.label: fragment(): runs once for each pixel the shape covers
COLOR: the color of the pixel being drawn

props.videoLabel: Godot 4.7.2 · Forward+ · a ColorRect with no image of its own

shot.motion_claim: The ring hops to a cell, and its address and color are read out.

lecture.why: Code and its result side by side is the claim: one line fills the whole shape from a table the shape never owned.
lecture.capture_spec: C02: Lab rect 360x360 logical, lab-shaders/01-lookup.gdshader, --tex tex=checker, still PNG at 4K. Verified probes: (0.06, 0.06) = (0.980, 0.977, 0.961) cream; (0.19, 0.06) = (0.372, 0.639, 0.569) teal.

beats.narration_text: Where does the table come from? A uniform of type sampler two D is a slot you fill from outside. Any texture fits: a small picture, a gradient, noise. It stretches across the shape, because the address always runs from zero to one.

shot.visual_intent: Code card at left with the uniform line highlighted. At right the same real Godot window shows three tables in turn with no change to the code: the small cream F on teal (smeared, because it is tiny), the red-green gradient, the grey noise. A caption under the window says 'same code'.

cues.label: uniform: a value your game sets from outside
sampler2D: the type of a texture a shader reads

beats.narration_text: That small picture came out smeared. An address can land between two entries, and by default the graphics card blends the four nearest. Add filter nearest, and it takes the closest entry only: crisp blocks, which is what pixel art wants.

shot.visual_intent: Code card at left with the hint highlighted. At right two real panels of the small F table side by side: on the left the smeared default, on the right the crisp blocks after the hint. Panel labels 'default' and 'filter_nearest'.

beats.narration_text: Because it is a lookup, you can ask for any address you like. Ask for one minus the horizontal address, and the picture flips. The table never changed. Only where you looked.

shot.visual_intent: Code card at left with the address line highlighted. At right two real panels: the F table as it is, then, beside it, the same table flipped left to right (the F's stem moves from left to right). Labels 'same table' and 'new address'.

beats.narration_text: Ask for twice the address, and half the lookups fall off the end of the table. With repeat disable, the edge entries stretch outward. With repeat enable, the table starts over, and tiles.

beats.narration_text: What comes back from a lookup is a vec four: four numbers, each from zero to one. Red, green, blue, and alpha. Orange is one, one half, zero, one. A color is only numbers, so you can do arithmetic on it.

shot.visual_intent: Act title 'Color Is Math' (serif 40) top-left. A large orange swatch (1.0, 0.5, 0.0, 1.0) with four labelled bars beside it, R G B A, each an outline track with a terracotta dot at its value. A label 'vec4: a bundle of four numbers'. The G bar slides up to 0.9 and the swatch turns yellow-orange; the B bar slides to 0.4 and it pales.

shot.motion_claim: Sliding one bar changes the swatch: the color is nothing but the four numbers.

beats.narration_text: A sprite brings a table of its own, named texture, in capitals. Before your code runs, color already holds that lookup, multiplied by the node's modulate. Overwrite color with a plain lookup, and the modulate is thrown away.

shot.visual_intent: Code card at left (COLOR = texture(TEXTURE, UV)). At right two real panels of the four-patch picture on a sprite whose modulate is 50 % gray: on the left an empty fragment (the picture is darker), on the right the plain lookup (the picture is full bright). Labels 'empty: keeps modulate' and 'plain lookup: drops it'.

cues.label: a plain lookup: the modulate is gone

props.videoLabel: Godot 4.7.2 · Forward+ · node modulate 50 % gray · two renders
props.caption: COLOR starts as the picture times modulate, the node's tint color

shot.motion_claim: The right panel jumps to full brightness as the plain lookup throws the modulate away.

beats.narration_text: Multiply the color by a tint. A channel times one stays, times a half it halves. This tint keeps all the red, most of the green, and half the blue, so the picture turns warm.

shot.visual_intent: Code card at left (a tint color multiplied into COLOR.rgb). At right the real four-patch picture, untouched, then the shader is switched on and every patch warms: the rose deepens, the sky patch turns slate. A readout '1.0, 0.7, 0.5' (the tint) appears.

beats.narration_text: One minus the color flips it. Zero becomes one, one becomes zero, and a half stays put. Do it to red, green and blue, and every patch turns into its opposite.

beats.narration_text: Careful with the fourth number. Flip alpha too, and the sprite turns see-through, while the empty space around it becomes a solid white card. Alpha is a channel like the others: only a number.

beats.narration_text: Add instead of multiply, and the picture brightens. Add a ramp that grows to one, and every patch ends in flat white. Ordinary two-D drawing cuts every number off at one, so the extra is lost.

beats.narration_text: To make gray, give red, green and blue the same number. The crude way copies one channel. Copy red, and the rose turns bright, while the leaf and the sky turn dark.

shot.visual_intent: Code card at left (gray = COLOR.r, then vec3(gray)). At right the real four-patch picture, untouched, then switched to gray: rose and sand turn light gray, leaf and sky turn a much darker gray. Readouts on three patches: 0.90, 0.40, 0.40.

props.videoLabel: Godot 4.7.2 · Forward+ · shader switched on by script

beats.narration_text: Better: weigh the channels by how bright each looks to the eye. About twenty-one percent red, seventy-two percent green, seven percent blue. Dot multiplies and adds them up. Now the rose, the leaf and the sky land on close grays.

shot.visual_intent: Code card at left (gray = dot(COLOR.rgb, vec3(0.2126, 0.7152, 0.0722))). At right two real panels of the four-patch picture in gray: on the left the crude red-channel version, on the right the weighted one where the rose, the leaf and the sky land on close grays and sand stays lightest. Readouts 0.48, 0.58, 0.51 on the weighted panel.

beats.narration_text: Mix blends two colors by an amount from zero to one. Here it blends the picture with its own gray: zero is all color, one is all gray. The amount can be one number for everything, or a different number at every pixel.

shot.visual_intent: Code card at left (an amount uniform; mix of the color and its gray). At right the real four-patch picture draining of its color as the amount sweeps from 0 to 1, a thin 0 to 1 strip under the window with a marker riding the amount.

show.event: mix line highlighted; the sweep starts

cues.label: mix: blends from a to b: t of 0 gives a, 1 gives b

lecture.why: A sweep with its marker is what 'an amount from zero to one' means; stills would lose the continuity.

beats.narration_text: Not every texture is a picture. This one is noise: soft clouds made of numbers, one from zero to one at every pixel. Read each number as an amount of teal, and you have a mask: how much of something to show.

shot.visual_intent: Act title 'Noise as a Mask' (serif 40) top-left. Code card at left (COLOR.a = the noise value). At right a real Godot window: a teal Color Rect whose opacity follows the noise, so soft teal clouds fade into the stage. Three readouts on three spots: 0.08 (nearly nothing), 0.50, 0.91 (nearly solid teal).

show.event: alpha line: mask, how much to show

cues.label: mask: a number from 0 to 1 per pixel, how much to show

props.videoLabel: Godot 4.7.2 · Forward+ · a teal Color Rect, alpha = noise

lecture.why: Real clouds with real numbers at three pixels show that a texture can be a map of amounts; teal-on-stage has no near-black pixels.

beats.narration_text: You do not draw it. In the Inspector, open the slot's menu and choose Noise Texture two D under New. Click it, then open its Noise slot the same way, and choose Fast Noise Lite. Godot generates the clouds, at the size and seed you choose.

One terracotta ring on the row or entry being named.

beats.narration_text: So the rule is short. Hint every color you give a shader, uniform or texture. Never hint a mask. And if you ship on more than one renderer, look at each, because a number read from one may not hold in the others.

beats.narration_text: Let's recap with Claude. A texture is a table you look up by address. A color is four numbers, so you can tint it, flip it, gray it and mix it. A noise texture is a mask: compare it with a threshold, and a sprite dissolves. The number you type is not always the color you see: there are two scales. Hint every color with source color, and never hint a mask. A number read from one renderer may not hold in another.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude: Write a Godot canvas item shader that dissolves a sprite. A noise texture decides which pixels go first, a float uniform called progress from zero to one is the dial, and a ramp texture colors the burning edge. Mark which texture needs the source color hint, and say why. Then check two things yourself. At progress zero, is the sprite untouched, and at one, is it gone? And does the ramp carry the source color hint, while the noise does not?
